hints: Focus on what makes a reaction fast on this diagram, the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy.
Notice that $T_2$ is lower at the peak but stretches further to the right, so $T_2$ is the higher temperature with more high-energy molecules.
Combine the higher temperature with the smaller energy barrier, $E_{A(1)}$, to maximise the fraction of molecules that can react.
walkthrough:
**Identify the higher temperature**

Remember, raising temperature flattens the peak and shifts the distribution to higher energy. Here $T_1$ is taller and narrower, while $T_2$ is shorter, broader and shifted right.

So: $T_2 > T_1$

**Identify the lower activation energy**

Only molecules with energy $\ge E_A$ can react on collision. On the energy axis, $E_{A(1)}$ is to the left of $E_{A(2)}$.

So: $$E_{A(1)} < E_{A(2)}$$

**Maximise the successful fraction**

Rate depends on the proportion of molecules beyond $E_A$. A higher $T$ pushes more molecules to high energy, and a lower $E_A$ makes the barrier easier to cross.

Therefore the fastest rate needs the higher temperature together with the lower activation energy, which is $T_2$ and $E_{A(1)}$.

options.A: T1 is the lower temperature, so fewer molecules have high energy. Even with the lower barrier EA(1), the successful fraction is smaller than at T2.
options.B: This is the worst combination. T1 is the lower temperature and EA(2) is the higher barrier, so the area beyond EA is smallest and the rate is lowest.
options.C: T2 is correctly the higher temperature, but EA(2) is the higher barrier. Many molecules still cannot reach this larger EA, so the rate is slower than with EA(1).
options.D: T2 is the higher temperature (broader, flatter curve) and EA(1) is the lower activation energy. This gives the largest area under the curve beyond EA, so the greatest proportion of successful collisions and the highest rate.
